d: To cleanse, purify, either ceremonially, actually, or morally.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, iMperative, second, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to purify”—to make clean or free from defilement. It describes an action rather than a person or object, and its exact force depends on what is being purified in the surrounding passage. The word occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, including passages connected with ceremonial cleansing and with the cleansing of people’s hearts and lives. Its repeated rendering as “purify” supports this central sense without requiring a broader or different meaning.

d: Disposed to form sects, sectarian, heretical, factious.
me: Adjective, Accusative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word describes someone or something that creates division, especially by separating people into opposing groups. Its central idea is being divisive or schismatic rather than promoting unity. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Titus 3:10. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to a person characterized by factional separation or conduct that produces division.

d: To salt, sprinkle with salt (of sacrifices or of those who offer sacrifice), keep fresh and sound, and so acceptable to God.
me: Verb, Future, Passive, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to salt,” describing the act of applying salt or being treated with salt. It is a verb expressing what happens when something is salted. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 5:13 and Mark 9:49. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central meaning remains the same: salt is applied to something, producing the condition of being salted.

d: To call out, shout, exclaim.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to exclaim”—to cry out or speak with a strong, noticeable expression. It describes an outward vocal response rather than a quiet thought or ordinary statement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 1:42, so its normal sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word focuses on the act of calling out or expressing something aloud with emphasis.

d: To set oneself against, oppose.
me: Verb, Present, Middle, Participle, Accusative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to oppose”: it describes actively setting oneself against someone or something rather than agreeing with it. It functions as an action word, expressing opposition. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 2 Timothy 2:25. The reference identifies its only occurrence, but the surrounding verse text is not included here, so the exact force in that sentence must be understood from its context.

e.t: This word means “to answer” or “to respond,” describing a person speaking in reply to what someone else has said or done. It commonly introduces a spoken response in the New Testament, often rendered “answered” when referring to a completed reply. The word appears 231 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that it is a common way to present dialogue and responses. Its exact force—whether a simple reply or a fuller response—depends on the surrounding sentence and conversation.

d: To cause to sink; to sink, submerge, drown.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, Present, Passive, iNfinitive

e.t: This word means “to plunge” or “to sink,” describing movement downward into or beneath something. It can refer to something descending physically, and its basic sense can also describe being brought into a condition of ruin or deep trouble when the surrounding context supports that use. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Luke 5:7 and 1 Timothy 6:9. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

d: The knee.
me: Noun, Accusative, Plural, Neuter
Noun, Accusative, Singular, Neuter

Noun, Nominative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This word means “a knee,” the joint between the thigh and lower leg. It is a noun and may refer to one knee or to knees in the plural. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times across 12 verses, including passages that mention people kneeling or falling upon their knees. The basic meaning remains physical and straightforward; the surrounding verse determines what action or posture involving the knees is being described.

d: Eber, father of Peleg and son of Shelah.
me: Noun, Genitive, Singular, Masculine, Person

e.t: Eber is a personal name, referring to a person identified by that name. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Luke 3:35. The word functions as a name rather than as a description, action, or quality. Its appearance in that verse should therefore be understood as identifying Eber within the passage’s recorded line of names. The name itself does not express a general spiritual or moral concept apart from the context in which it appears.

d: To go in, enter (originally: to shall go in).
me: Verb, Imperfect, Active, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, Present, Active, iNfinitive

e.t: This word means “to enter” or “to go in,” describing movement from outside into a place. It presents entering as an action, rather than naming the place or explaining why someone enters. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Acts and Hebrews. Its uses include people going into a place and priests going into the first section of the tabernacle, but the exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: Rebuke, reproof, refutation.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This word means “rebuke”: a firm expression of disapproval intended to correct someone. It refers to confronting wrong conduct or error rather than quietly overlooking it. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears once, in 2 Peter 2:16, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated uses within that corpus. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is a corrective reproof directed toward what is wrong.

d: To bless (of God).
me: Verb, Future, Passive, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “be blessed” or “to be blessed.” It describes people receiving blessing, focusing on the condition or result of being blessed rather than naming the blessing itself. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Acts 3:25 and once in Galatians 3:8. Its precise emphasis in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the receiving of blessing.

d: To have on over (as a garment); to put on oneself in addition.
me: Verb, Aorist, Middle, iNfinitive

e.t: This word means “be clothed” or “to be clothed with.” It describes putting clothing on oneself or being covered with something like a garment. As a verb, it expresses the act or condition of being clothed rather than naming the clothing itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Corinthians 5. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains being clothed or covered.

d: To contend, dispute, wrangle, strive.
me: Verb, Future, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to quarrel,” referring to arguing or engaging in a dispute. It describes conflict expressed through contentious speech or behavior rather than quiet disagreement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 12:19. Because it appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its exact force in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself; its basic meaning remains an act of quarreling or disputing.

d: Already; now at length, now after all this waiting.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “already” or “now”. It marks something as having happened by a given point (“already”) or identifies the present time (“now”). As a time word, it helps readers notice whether an action or condition is viewed as present, completed, or reached at that moment. It occurs 61 times in the Greek New Testament, so its basic force appears across many kinds of sentences rather than belonging to one special topic. The surrounding words determine whether “already” or “now” best expresses the timing in a particular verse.

d: To have come, to be present, have arrived.

e.t: This word means “to come” or “to be present.” It describes someone arriving, becoming present, or being expected to arrive. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 26 times and is commonly rendered “come.” Its sense can point to a person’s arrival, the presence of someone who has come, or the time when an expected arrival takes place. The surrounding sentence determines which aspect is most prominent.

d: Iota, a small letter of the Greek alphabet, used in the NT to indicate the smallest part.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: Iota refers to the smallest letter, and thus names something extremely small or minimal. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 5:18. Its basic sense is a tiny written letter; its use can therefore serve as a precise way to speak about even the smallest detail. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular force there, but the word itself points to the smallest letter rather than to a broad category or general idea.

d: Burning heat, heat.

e.t: This word means “heat,” referring to intense warmth or burning conditions. It is a noun that names the heat itself rather than describing an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Revelation, and is rendered “heat” in each occurrence. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the particular force of the word in either passage, but its basic meaning remains the experience or presence of strong heat.

d: (a) sing. and plural: bosom; (sinus) the overhanging fold of the garment used as a pocket, (b) a bay, gulf.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine
Noun, Dative, Plural, Masculine
Noun, Dative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “bosom,” referring to the chest or breast area. It can also describe the place close against someone’s chest, expressing nearness, welcome, or intimate association. As a noun, it identifies a physical location and can serve in descriptions of close personal position. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, in Luke, John, and Acts. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: Crispus, ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, converted and baptized by Paul.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine, Person
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine, Person

e.t: Crispus is a personal name, referring to a man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs twice: once in Acts 18:8 and once in 1 Corinthians 1:14. The name itself identifies the individual; its particular significance in either passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, not from the name alone.

d: (Aramaic), riches, money, possessions, property.
me: Noun, Dative, Singular, Masculine
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “wealth”: material riches or possessions. It refers to what a person has in the realm of money and property, rather than to an inward quality or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, in Matthew and Luke. Its normal sense concerns material resources that may be owned, valued, or used. The precise force of the word in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: Meanwhile, afterwards, between.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined
PREPosition

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “between” and can also describe what happens “meanwhile.” It points to a position or interval separating people, places, things, or events. In a sentence, it may mark what lies between two sides, or indicate that something occurs during the time before another event. The word appears nine times in the New Testament, so its central idea remains consistent while its exact force depends on whether the sentence describes location, separation, or timing.

e.t: This word refers to a lawyer or an expert in the law—someone recognized for knowledge of legal requirements. In the Greek New Testament, it is used for people whose role involved understanding and handling the law. The word appears nine times in nine New Testament verses, especially in Luke, and is also used in Matthew and Titus. Its basic sense identifies a person connected with legal expertise; the surrounding passage determines whether the person is simply being identified by role or is being addressed because of how that knowledge is used.

d: To trouble, torment, worry, vex.
me: Verb, Present, Passive, Participle, Accusative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to be tormented” or “to disturb,” describing a person who is troubled or afflicted. It presents disturbance as something that presses heavily on someone, rather than a calm or minor inconvenience. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 5:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is serious distress or disturbance.

d: (a) to hear carelessly or incidentally, or to pretend not to hear, (b) to refuse to hear; to disobey, disregard.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine
Verb, Aorist, Active, Subjunctive, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to ignore” or “to refuse to listen.” It describes a deliberate response in which someone disregards what another person says rather than heeding it. Thus, it points beyond simply failing to hear; it emphasizes unwillingness to listen or give attention. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, across two verses, and consistently centers on refusing to respond to spoken instruction or words. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: To sail past (without stopping there).
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, iNfinitive

e.t: This word means “to sail past,” describing the action of traveling by water beyond or alongside a place. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The central idea is movement by water past a location. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 20:16. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on sailing past.

d: To put on a spit; to pierce, wound deeply.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This word means “to pierce,” describing the act of penetrating or thrusting through something. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Timothy 6:10. That single occurrence establishes its basic meaning, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain precisely how the action is being presented there. The word therefore points to piercing as a direct, forceful action rather than merely touching or approaching.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to manage” or “to set before.” It describes taking responsibility for directing, arranging, or caring for something placed under one’s oversight. The word is used eight times in the Greek New Testament, especially in passages concerning the proper care of a household, leadership, and service among believers. Its basic emphasis is active oversight: bringing matters into order and giving them responsible direction. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: To frighten, terrify.
me: Verb, Present, Passive, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word describes being frightened or causing someone else to be frightened. It can therefore express either the experience of fear or the act of frightening another person, depending on how it is used in a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 1:28. Its precise force there belongs to the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is fear expressed either as a person’s response or as an action that produces fear.

d: Hard, violent, harsh, stern.
me: Adjective, Genitive, Plural, Masculine
Adjective, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

Adjective, Nominative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This word means “hard,” describing something difficult, demanding, severe, or resistant rather than easy or gentle. Its basic sense can apply to a matter that is difficult to accept, an action that is difficult to perform, or a condition that offers resistance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, so its meaning is focused and consistent rather than broadly varied across many passages. The surrounding words determine the particular kind of hardness intended in each occurrence.

d: (to keep someone in a tight place), to press upon, cramp, restrain.
me: Verb, Present, Passive, Indicative, second, Plural
Verb, Present, Passive, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word describes being crushed, tightly pressed, or hemmed in by pressure. It can portray a person who feels constrained or burdened rather than physically free to move. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in 2 Corinthians, where it expresses pressure without implying that the person has been completely destroyed. Its central idea is intense restriction or distress pressing against someone. The precise force in each occurrence comes from its surrounding sentence, but the word itself points to being pressed hard or brought into a cramped condition.

d: A completion, consummation, end; a joint payment (for public service).
me: Noun, Dative, Singular, Feminine
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Feminine
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word refers to the “end” or “consummation”—the point at which something reaches its final completion. In the Greek New Testament, it is used six times, especially in Matthew and once in Hebrews. It can describe the end of an age, the completion of a period, or the final point toward which events move. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being discussed.

d: A conspiracy, plot.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means a plot: a planned scheme formed by several people, usually for a harmful or unlawful purpose. It refers to the coordinated plan itself rather than to one isolated action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Acts 23:13. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from its context; its basic meaning remains a deliberate, joined plan against someone or something.

me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Feminine, Location Gentilic

e.t: This word refers to a woman from Syrian Phoenicia, identifying her by her regional and ethnic background. It is a descriptive name rather than a general word for every woman, and its meaning is “Syrophoenician” or “woman of Syrian Phoenicia.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Mark 7:26. The word therefore identifies the woman in that passage by where her people were from; the specific significance of her encounter must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

d: To insult, treat with insolence.

e.t: This word means to insult or mistreat someone—to treat a person with contempt, abuse, or dishonor. It describes harmful treatment expressed through words or actions, rather than simple disagreement or inconvenience. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including passages describing people being treated shamefully and others being insulted or mistreated. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

d: Answerable to, liable to (brought under) the judgment of.
me: Adjective, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “accountable,” describing someone who must answer for what has been done. It points to responsibility before judgment rather than merely recognizing that an action occurred. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Romans 3:19, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its central idea remains clear: a person is liable to give an account and cannot claim to stand outside the standard by which conduct is judged.

d: Height, barrier, bulwark; presumption.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Neuter
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: “Height” refers to elevated position or stature—the upward dimension of something. In the Greek New Testament, this noun appears twice, so its basic meaning is focused and consistent rather than broad or varied. It occurs in Romans 8:39 and 2 Corinthians 10:5. The word identifies height as a thing or reality, while the surrounding verse determines its precise force. Its central idea remains elevation: being high, raised, or above.

d: A bridle, bit.
me: Noun, Accusative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means a bit or bridle—the device placed in a horse’s mouth to guide and control it. It refers to an instrument of direction and restraint, rather than to the horse itself or the person guiding it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in James and once in Revelation. Its listed meanings include “bit,” “bridle,” and “bridles,” with the exact wording shaped by the sentence in which it appears.

e.t: This word means “to announce” or “to warn,” describing the communication of a message, instruction, or caution. Its wording can refer to someone announcing what has been made known, or warning others about what they should understand or do. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, so its meaning is established across several passages rather than being limited to one setting. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

d: A falsehood, lie, untruthfulness.
me: Noun, Dative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “falsehood”—something untrue, deceptive, or contrary to what is true. It functions as a noun, naming the false statement or claim itself rather than describing the person who speaks it. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 3:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding argument, but its basic meaning remains a falsehood: an assertion that does not correspond to truth.
